jones_burd_2001.citation: Jones A & Burd M (2001). Vegetative and reproductive variation among unisexual and hermaphroditic individuals of Wurmbea dioica (Colchicaceae). Australian Journal of Botany 49:603-609.
jones_burd_2001.study_level: Published author abstract; full article and raw records not independently obtained
jones_burd_2001.unit_warning: Flower-level morphology-controlled contrasts and whole-plant totals are distinct; not an experimental manipulation of conflict nor a fitness estimate

ramsey_vaughton_2001.citation: Ramsey M & Vaughton G (2001). Sex Expression and Sexual Dimorphism in Subdioecious Wurmbea dioica (Colchicaceae). International Journal of Plant Sciences 162:589-597.
ramsey_vaughton_2001.geography: Eastern Australian subdioecious populations; three populations in source abstract
ramsey_vaughton_2001.study_level: Published abstract only; no access to individual original observations
ramsey_vaughton_2001.warning: Published authors' summarized comparisons; no new confidence interval, genotype fitness, historical direction or independent raw cohort analysis

case_et_al_2008.citation: Case AL, Graham SW, Macfarlane TD & Barrett SCH (2008). A Phylogenetic Study of Evolutionary Transitions in Sexual Systems in Australasian Wurmbea (Colchicaceae). International Journal of Plant Sciences 169:141-156.
case_et_al_2008.molecular_data: Four non-contiguous plastid regions, 5,337 aligned nt across taxon set
case_et_al_2008.sexual_system_states: Gender monomorphic vs gender dimorphic; NOT 4-state functional architectures
case_et_al_2008.bottom_line: Multiple state differences on plastid gene tree; repeated transitions direction and number of actual species-level origins cannot be confidently assigned

goldberg_et_al_2017.citation: Goldberg EE, Otto SP, Vamosi JC, Mayrose I, Sabath N, Ming R & Ashman TL (2017). Macroevolutionary synthesis of flowering plant sexual systems. Evolution 71:898-912.
goldberg_et_al_2017.inclusion_frame: Genera with at least 10 species with known sexual system, at least two sexual systems and at least two H or two D taxa; not representative of all flowering plants
goldberg_et_al_2017.source_verified: Publisher and author-PDF abstract and original Figure 1/2 screenshots

western_taxonomy_status_2026.accepted_taxon_database: Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens Kew
western_taxonomy_status_2026.alternative_hypothesis_source: Genomics for Australian Plants conservation genomics project initiated August 2020
western_taxonomy_status_2026.potential_issue: Western subsp. alba complex may be multiple distinct taxa outside W. dioica s.str.; no published taxonomic resolution documented here
western_taxonomy_status_2026.evidence_latest: Western Australia DBCA 2024-25 science report (published 2026) notes Wurmbea dioica conservation genetic project well advanced, not settled

interpretation_limits: Flower-level allocation compromise in one eastern population does not demonstrate adaptive genetic origin or an SLK G1 conflict estimator
Published male/female/fruiting-male group comparisons are not plant-level matched longitudinal genomic data across separate studies
Western subsp. alba and eastern W. dioica s.str. should not be merged into one genetic evolutionary trajectory; taxonomy remains under study
An ambiguous plastid phylogeny is not evidence that any organ re-evolved after genetic deletion
Genome-project proposal and Kew accepted name report different evidential states and do not independently prove current taxonomic revision
No phylogenetic independent origin count, W_s/W_p/W_d, Phi, g0 or Delta_R has been estimated by this source synthesis
The 2017 macro analysis sampled genera polymorphic for sexual system, not a random global set, and its H/G/M/D states are not interchangeable with SLK architecture labels
This receipt is not new experimental evidence, causal meta-analysis, reanalysis of the 2017 Dryad archive, or a combined pooled standardized effect size
